p.x:
Yesterday, we had a great science lesson. Our teacher, Mr Somchai, showed us an experiment. First, he put some ice in a metal pan and heated it. After two minutes, the ice started to melt and became a liquid. Then the water started to boil, and we saw steam rising into the air. "Steam is a gas," Mr Somchai explained.
Next, we used a thermometer to measure the temperature of the water. It was 100 degrees! Mr Somchai said that a famous scientist called Anders Celsius created this temperature scale almost 300 years ago.
At the end of the lesson, we talked about light and sound. Mr Somchai asked, "Why do we see lightning before we hear thunder?" Nobody knew. Then he told us: light travels much faster than sound! I can't wait for the next lesson.

Dr Anong is a biologist who works in a university laboratory in Bangkok. Her research focuses on rice plants and how they can survive with less water. "With climate change, farmers need rice that can grow during long dry periods," she explains.
Her day starts at 8 a.m. First, she checks the plants growing in the lab under special lights. Then she takes small samples of their leaves and examines them under a microscope. She also uses a machine to measure the chemicals inside each plant. All the data goes into a computer, where she compares the results from different types of rice.
"Science is slow," she says. "You have a theory, you test it, and most of the time it doesn't work. But when it does, it's the best feeling in the world." Last year, her team discovered that one type of rice grows deeper roots that reach water more easily. This could become an important invention for farmers in the future.
In her free time, Dr Anong enjoys looking at the night sky through a telescope. "It reminds me how small we are," she says. "Gravity holds the whole universe together, but we still don't fully understand it." She also keeps one solid rule: never take work home at the weekend.

Many people imagine science as a series of sudden breakthroughs made by lonely geniuses. In reality, most scientific progress is slow and collaborative. It usually begins with an observation: someone notices a strange phenomenon, such as bacteria failing to grow near a particular mould. The scientist then forms a hypothesis that might explain it and designs experiments to test it.
Modern experiments can be extraordinarily precise. Researchers study individual molecules, track particles moving at nearly the speed of light, and read the genetic code of entire organisms. Yet the basic method remains the same: collect data, analyse it carefully, and see whether the results support the hypothesis.
Crucially, results must be checked by other scientists before they are accepted. This process, known as peer review, helps catch mistakes and prevent false claims. History shows why it matters. In the early twentieth century, radiation was thought to be healthy, and some companies sold radioactive drinks. Only later did careful research reveal the terrible damage it could cause.
Science, then, is not a collection of fixed facts but a method for getting gradually closer to the truth, one that welcomes being proved wrong.

q.s: [Scientist] [works] [in] [a] laboratory.

q.th: หลัง 100 ต้องเป็นพหูพจน์: degrees

q.s: Metals [get] bigger [when] they [get] [heat].

q.s: The results [of] the experiment [was] [very] [surprising].

q.s: If you [will heat] ice, it [melts] [into] [water].
q.fix: If you heat ice, it melts into water.
q.en: Zero conditional (general facts): If + present, present. No 'will'.
q.th: zero conditional (ข้อเท็จจริง): If + ปัจจุบัน, ปัจจุบัน ไม่ใช้ will

q.s: The experiment [was] [repeated] [three] [time].

q.en: 'Time' meaning occasion is countable: three times.
q.th: time (ครั้ง) นับได้: three times

q.s: The bacteria [is] [growing] [quickly] [in] the warm dish.

q.th: bacteria เป็นพหูพจน์ (เอกพจน์คือ bacterium): are

q.s: Hardly had the scientists [published] their results [than] other labs [tried] [to copy] them.
q.fix: Hardly had the scientists published their results when other labs tried to copy them.
q.en: 'Hardly' goes with 'when' (or 'before'), not 'than'. ('No sooner' goes with 'than'.)
q.th: hardly ใช้คู่กับ when ไม่ใช่ than (no sooner ใช้คู่กับ than)
